content: An emulsion is a mixture of two substances that do not naturally blend together, known as immiscible substances. In an emulsion, one substance, called the dispersed phase, is distributed throughout another substance, referred to as the continuous phase. Examples of emulsions include butter, margarine, milk, cream, espresso, mayonnaise, photographic film coatings, certain types of magma, and cutting fluids used in metalworking. In butter and margarine, water droplets are dispersed within an oil matrix, forming a water-in-oil emulsion. Conversely, in milk and cream, oil droplets are dispersed within a water matrix, creating an oil-in-water emulsion. In some magmas, liquid nickel-iron globules are dispersed within a continuous phase of liquid silicates. The process of creating an emulsion is called emulsification. In the oil industry, the term emulsion is also used to describe untreated well production that primarily consists of crude oil and water. Emulsions typically appear cloudy because the numerous interfaces between the dispersed and continuous phases scatter light. These mixtures are inherently unstable and do not form spontaneously. Energy input, such as shaking, stirring, homogenization, or spraying, is required to create an emulsion. Over time, emulsions tend to separate into their original components, with oil and water separating into distinct layers. However, the addition of surface-active agents, known as surfactants, can significantly enhance the kinetic stability of emulsions, allowing them to remain stable for extended periods, even years. For example, homemade oil-and-vinegar salad dressings are unstable emulsions that quickly separate unless continuously shaken. This separation process, known as coalescence, occurs when smaller droplets merge to form larger ones. Emulsions can also experience creaming, where one phase migrates to the top of the mixture due to buoyancy or centrifugal forces. Emulsions belong to a broader category of two-phase systems called colloids. While the terms colloid and emulsion are sometimes used interchangeably, emulsions specifically refer to systems where both the dispersed and continuous phases are liquids. Emulsion instability can manifest in three primary ways: flocculation, where particles clump together; creaming, where particles concentrate at the surface or bottom of the mixture while remaining separate; and breaking or coalescence, where particles merge to form a distinct liquid layer. An emulsifier, also known as an emulgent, is a substance that stabilizes an emulsion, often by acting as a surfactant. Common food emulsifiers include egg yolk, which contains lecithin as its primary emulsifying agent, as well as honey and mustard, which contain various emulsifying chemicals in the mucilage surrounding mustard seeds. Proteins and low-molecular-weight emulsifiers are also frequently used. In some cases, solid particles can stabilize emulsions through a mechanism known as Pickering stabilization. For example, mayonnaise and hollandaise sauce are oil-in-water emulsions stabilized by lecithin from egg yolks. Detergents, another class of surfactants, chemically interact with both oil and water, stabilizing the interface between oil and water droplets. This principle is utilized in soaps to remove grease during cleaning. In pharmaceutical applications, a wide range of emulsifiers is used to prepare emulsions such as creams and lotions. Whether an emulsion forms as a water-in-oil or oil-in-water system depends on the relative volume fractions of the two phases and the type of emulsifier used. According to the Bancroft rule, emulsifiers tend to promote the dispersion of the phase in which they are less soluble. For instance, proteins, which are more soluble in water than in oil, typically promote the formation of oil-in-water emulsions, where oil droplets are dispersed in a continuous water phase. A nanoemulsion is a specialized type of emulsion in which the dispersed phase consists of particles smaller than 1000 nanometers in diameter. In medical applications, nanoemulsions of soybean oil, with droplet sizes ranging from 400 to 600 nanometers, have been shown to kill various pathogens, including bacteria and viruses. This process is physical rather than chemical. The small droplet size increases surface tension, creating a strong force that drives the droplets to merge with other lipids. The oil droplets are stabilized with detergents to prevent them from merging with each other. When these droplets encounter lipid membranes, such as those of bacteria or viruses, they force the lipids to merge with the droplets, effectively disrupting the membrane and killing the pathogen. Importantly, this type of nanoemulsion does not harm normal human cells or the cells of most higher organisms. However, certain cell types, such as sperm cells and blood cells, are vulnerable to nanoemulsions due to their specific membrane structures. As a result, these nanoemulsions are not yet suitable for intravenous use. The most effective application of this technology is for surface disinfection. Some nanoemulsions have demonstrated the ability to destroy pathogens such as HIV-1 and tuberculosis bacteria on non-porous surfaces.
